I am 68 years old, and I have farmed my land in Quzhou County for more than 40 years. My family has always lived here, and I know every mu of my 8 mu of flat, irrigated land. I only finished primary school, but I know this land better than any book.

This year, I will stick to what has always worked: **winter wheat followed by summer maize** on the same 8 mu. That is the rotation everyone in my village trusts. The wheat is already in the ground from last October. In March I will topdress it with urea and irrigate it through the spring. After I harvest the wheat in early June, I will immediately plant maize without tilling — we call this "no-tillage" sowing, and it saves time and keeps the soil moist in the hot summer.

I buy **improved Jimai wheat seeds** from the village agro-store. For maize, I only use **Denghai hybrid seeds**; they cost more, but the yield is worth it. I rotary-till before wheat sowing, but maize gets no tillage — I learned long ago that turning the soil twice a year dries it out.

For fertilizer, I apply compound fertilizer as a basal dose and topdress with urea. On the wheat, I use about 19 kg of nitrogen per mu, plus phosphorus and potassium from the compound bag. On the maize I use less, about 11 kg nitrogen per mu, because the wheat stubble still has some goodness in it. I irrigate wheat four times — winter water, green-up, jointing, and grain filling — and maize twice, at the jointing and tasseling stages. I spray pesticides three times for each crop: herbicide once, and insecticide twice when the bugs come.

I thought about planting cotton on 2 mu like some of my neighbors, but I decided against it. At my age, bending down to spray cotton 15 or 16 times a season is too hard on my back. Wheat and maize can be harvested by machine, and that is what I need now.
